lessonTitle: Perioperative Complications: Anaphylaxis, Hypotension and Malignant Hyperthermia

blocks.text: Four minutes after induction of anaesthesia in a 34-year-old woman for a laparoscopic gynaecological procedure, the blood pressure becomes unrecordable, the heart rate rises to 140/min, the airway pressure climbs, and a flush spreads across her chest. The monitor, rather than the patient, makes the diagnosis first; the anaesthetist's task is to recognise the pattern and act within seconds.

blocks.markdown: **Perioperative anaphylaxis (objective 1).** Anaphylaxis is a severe, life-threatening systemic hypersensitivity reaction, usually IgE mediated, in which mast cell and basophil degranulation releases histamine, tryptase and other mediators. Under anaesthesia the patient cannot report symptoms, so presentation is by signs: hypotension or cardiovascular collapse, tachycardia (or bradycardia), bronchospasm with high airway pressure and falling end-tidal CO2, and skin changes (flushing, urticaria, angioedema), which may be absent or late. Common triggers in UK audit (NAP6) include neuromuscular blocking drugs, antibiotics (such as teicoplanin and co-amoxiclav), and chlorhexidine; latex and dyes are also recognised. A new drug exposure within minutes of the event raises suspicion.

blocks.title: Management in outline (Resuscitation Council UK and Association of Anaesthetists guidance)
blocks.text: Call for help, stop the suspected trigger and any volatile agent, give 100% oxygen, and give adrenaline early: in an anaesthetised patient with intravenous access, small titrated intravenous boluses with continuous monitoring (for example 50 micrograms increments in adults) are advocated, with intramuscular adrenaline (0.5 mg of 1 in 1000 in adults) if there is no IV access. Give a rapid intravenous crystalloid fluid bolus. Chlorphenamine and hydrocortisone are second-line and do not replace adrenaline. Take serial mast cell tryptase samples, and refer for specialist allergy investigation. Check against current Resuscitation Council UK, Association of Anaesthetists, BNF and local guidance.

blocks.title: Adrenaline concentrations and volumes
blocks.prompt: Adrenaline is labelled as 1 in 1000, 1 in 10 000 and 1 in 100 000. Express each as mg/mL and calculate the volume containing (a) 0.5 mg of 1 in 1000 and (b) 50 micrograms of a 1 in 100 000 dilution (teaching example).

steps.text: A '1 in 1000' ratio means 1 g in 1000 mL, which is 1000 mg in 1000 mL.
Each ten-fold dilution reduces the concentration ten-fold.
(a) The intramuscular dose of 0.5 mg of 1 in 1000.

Mistaking 1 in 1000 for a dilute preparation and giving it intravenously is a recognised cause of harm, so label and check every syringe. Check against current Resuscitation Council UK, Association of Anaesthetists, BNF and local guidance.

blocks.answer: (a) 0.5 mL of 1 in 1000 for the intramuscular dose; (b) 5 mL of 1 in 100 000 for 50 micrograms.

blocks.markdown: **Aspiration of gastric contents.** Pulmonary aspiration is the passage of gastric contents into the lungs, most often at induction or emergence when airway reflexes are lost. Risk factors are emergency surgery, bowel obstruction, delayed gastric emptying, pregnancy, obesity with reflux and inadequate fasting. Acid causes a chemical pneumonitis (Mendelson syndrome); particulate matter obstructs airways and infection may follow. Features are regurgitation or vomit in the pharynx, bronchospasm, hypoxia and later infiltrates on chest radiograph. Immediate management: call for help, tilt the patient head down (or into the lateral position), suction the oropharynx, secure the airway and give 100% oxygen, then provide supportive care and an escalation of respiratory support as needed. Prevention uses fasting, rapid sequence induction with a trained assistant and suction in the 'at risk', and a plan for the airway.

**Intraoperative hypotension (objective 2).** Arterial pressure depends on cardiac output and systemic vascular resistance, and cardiac output on heart rate and stroke volume (preload, contractility, afterload). Hypotension therefore has causes in each term. Most intraoperative hypotension is predictable: vasodilatation and negative inotropy from anaesthetic drugs, the sympathetic block of neuraxial anaesthesia, hypovolaemia from bleeding, fasting or third-space loss, and reduced venous return (head-up position, positive pressure ventilation, pneumoperitoneum, aortocaval compression, caval clamping). Less common but dangerous causes include anaphylaxis, tension pneumothorax, pulmonary embolism, cardiac tamponade, myocardial infarction, arrhythmia and sepsis. Always treat the cause as well as the number.

rows: Propofol or volatile agents, neuraxial block, sepsis, anaphylaxis
Warm periphery; falls after drug or block
Bleeding, fasting and dehydration, pneumoperitoneum, aortocaval compression, positive pressure ventilation
Pulse pressure variation, low filling, falling ETCO2 with bleeding
Negative inotropes, myocardial ischaemia, bradycardia from vagal stimulation
Raised airway pressure or neck veins, sudden fall in ETCO2
blocks.caption: Causes of intraoperative hypotension by mechanism.
Mean arterial pressure (mmHg) estimated from systolic and diastolic values; a mean arterial pressure below about 65 mmHg is a commonly used threshold for concern, but targets are individualised.

blocks.title: Calculating MAP and thinking about cause
blocks.prompt: Under spinal anaesthesia for a knee replacement a patient's non-invasive pressure falls to 85/45 mmHg. Calculate the MAP and outline the response.

steps.text: Compare with the commonly used target of at least 65 mmHg (individualised): the value is low and warrants action.

Check the monitoring, give oxygen, and ask whether the cause is vasodilatation from the block, bleeding, or an obstructive or cardiac cause; treat with a vasopressor, fluids and positioning as indicated, and re-measure. Check against current Resuscitation Council UK, Association of Anaesthetists, BNF and local guidance.

blocks.answer: MAP about 58 mmHg: hypotension to treat, with cause-directed management.

blocks.markdown: **Malignant hyperthermia.** Malignant hyperthermia (MH) is a rare pharmacogenetic disorder of skeletal muscle (commonly a ryanodine receptor defect) triggered by volatile anaesthetics and suxamethonium, causing uncontrolled calcium release and a hypermetabolic crisis. The earliest signs are an unexplained rise in end-tidal CO2 despite increased ventilation, tachycardia and masseter spasm; temperature rise is often late. Management: stop all triggers, call for help, hyperventilate with 100% oxygen using a clean circuit, give dantrolene intravenously (initial bolus 2.5 mg/kg, repeated as needed; check the guideline for dosing), cool, and treat hyperkalaemia, acidosis and arrhythmias. Management follows the Association of Anaesthetists malignant hyperthermia guideline; check current Association of Anaesthetists, BNF and local guidance.

**Monitoring standards (objective 3).** The Association of Anaesthetists publishes standards for monitoring during anaesthesia and recovery (check the current edition). The principle is continuous presence of a trained anaesthetist and the same standard of monitoring from induction through recovery. Minimum monitoring includes pulse oximetry with an audible tone, electrocardiography, non-invasive blood pressure (at least every five minutes, more often when unstable), airway gases with continuous capnography in anyone receiving general anaesthesia or with a supraglottic or tracheal airway, inspired oxygen concentration, and agent concentration when a volatile agent is used. Temperature is measured in longer cases, neuromuscular function when relaxants are used, and depth of anaesthesia monitoring in total intravenous anaesthesia with muscle relaxants.

rows: Regular intervals, more often if unstable
Continuous waveform with tracheal tube, supraglottic airway or sedation
Continuous if an airway device remains in place
When relaxants are used; temperature in longer cases
Check recovery of function and temperature
blocks.caption: Monitoring during anaesthesia and recovery, summarised; check the current Association of Anaesthetists standards.

blocks.title: Monitors do not replace the clinician
blocks.text: Alarms are limited, artefacts occur and oxygen saturation can remain normal while ventilation fails. Look at the patient as well as the monitors, and respond to trends. A flat capnography waveform after intubation means the tube is not in the trachea until proved otherwise.

points: Anaphylaxis under anaesthesia presents with hypotension, bronchospasm and rash; remove the trigger, give oxygen, fluids and adrenaline early; take tryptase and refer for allergy testing.
Aspiration needs head-down positioning, suction, airway protection and oxygen; prevention relies on fasting and risk assessment.
Intraoperative hypotension arises from vasodilatation, reduced preload, reduced cardiac function or obstruction; MAP is about diastolic plus one third of pulse pressure.
Malignant hyperthermia presents with rising ETCO2, tachycardia and rigidity and is treated by stopping triggers and giving dantrolene.
Monitoring standards require continuous capnography, oximetry, ECG and blood pressure, with the same standard maintained into recovery.

questions.stem: During a knee arthroplasty a 62-year-old man develops profound hypotension, wheeze and facial flushing five minutes after an intravenous antibiotic is started. Which drug is the most important immediate treatment?

distractorRationale.b: Second-line and does not treat the shock or bronchospasm quickly.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: adrenaline is the first-line, life-saving drug in anaphylaxis.

questions.explanation: Adrenaline reverses the vasodilatation, increased capillary permeability and bronchospasm of anaphylaxis, and should be given early after stopping the trigger and calling for help. Antihistamines and steroids are adjuncts and should not delay it.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man with bowel obstruction regurgitates fluid into the pharynx during rapid sequence induction and the saturation begins to fall. Which is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Place a nasogastric tube before anything else
Tilt head down (or lateral), suction the oropharynx, secure the airway and give 100% oxygen
Insert an oral airway and ventilate vigorously with the facemask
Give a fluid bolus and wait

questions.correctOptionText: Tilt head down (or lateral), suction the oropharynx, secure the airway and give 100% oxygen

distractorRationale.b: Correct: positioning and suction limit further soiling while the airway is secured.
distractorRationale.c: Vigorous bag ventilation can push contents into the lungs.
distractorRationale.d: Does not deal with the contaminated airway.

questions.explanation: The priority is to prevent further contamination of the lower airway and oxygenate. Head-down tilt keeps fluid in the pharynx for suction, after which the airway is secured and ventilation supported.

questions.stem: A patient under sevoflurane for a hip operation has a blood pressure of 78/40 mmHg, heart rate 62/min, minimal blood loss and warm peripheries. Which cause is most likely?

options.text: Vasodilatation and myocardial depression from anaesthetic drugs

questions.correctOptionText: Vasodilatation and myocardial depression from anaesthetic drugs

distractorRationale.a: Usually causes sudden fall in ETCO2 and hypoxia.
distractorRationale.b: Would usually cause high airway pressure and neck vein distension.
distractorRationale.c: Would cause a small pulse pressure and raised venous pressure.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: drugs are the most common cause and the warm periphery suggests vasodilatation.

questions.explanation: Volatile and intravenous agents reduce vascular tone and contractility in a dose-dependent manner. With no blood loss and warm peripheries, drug effect is the most probable cause and is treated by reducing agent depth and using a vasopressor.

questions.stem: Which monitor is part of the minimum standard for a patient with a tracheal tube in place during general anaesthesia?

distractorRationale.c: Correct: capnography is mandatory for patients with an airway device.

questions.explanation: Capnography confirms ventilation and tube position and gives early warning of disconnection, obstruction and many circulatory events. Invasive pressure monitors are added according to patient and surgical risk.

questions.stem: After induction with sevoflurane and suxamethonium, a 20-year-old man develops masseter spasm, tachycardia and an end-tidal CO2 that continues to rise despite doubling minute ventilation. What is the most likely diagnosis and first action?

options.text: Light anaesthesia: increase the volatile concentration
Malignant hyperthermia: stop the volatile agent and call for help, then give dantrolene

questions.correctOptionText: Malignant hyperthermia: stop the volatile agent and call for help, then give dantrolene

distractorRationale.a: Increasing the volatile agent would worsen MH.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: classic hypermetabolic picture; triggers are stopped and treatment started.
distractorRationale.c: Anaphylaxis presents with hypotension and wheeze, with falling ETCO2.
distractorRationale.d: Would not raise ETCO2 despite ventilation.

questions.explanation: Unexplained rising end-tidal CO2 with tachycardia and masseter rigidity after triggering agents suggests malignant hyperthermia. The first step is to stop triggers and call for help, and dantrolene is the specific treatment; check current Association of Anaesthetists guidance.

questions.stem: Patients in recovery should be monitored to the same standard as during anaesthesia, with dedicated trained staff.
questions.explanation: Recovery is a high-risk period because airway reflexes, ventilation and circulation are still affected by anaesthetic and analgesic drugs. Association of Anaesthetists standards require continuous monitoring with trained staff until the patient is awake and stable; check the current edition.

questions.stem: An anaesthetist wishes to give 50 micrograms of adrenaline intravenously using a 1 in 10 000 solution (1 g in 10 000 mL). How many mL of this solution contain 50 micrograms? (Teaching example; check current guidance for real use.)
questions.explanation: A 1 in 10 000 solution contains 1 g in 10 000 mL, which is 0.1 mg/mL or 100 micrograms/mL. Therefore 50 micrograms is 50 / 100 = 0.5 mL.

questions.stem: A patient under general anaesthesia has a blood pressure of 96/54 mmHg. Estimate the mean arterial pressure in mmHg using diastolic plus one third of the pulse pressure.
questions.explanation: Pulse pressure is 96 - 54 = 42 mmHg and one third of this is 14 mmHg. MAP is 54 + 14 = 68 mmHg, which is above the commonly used threshold of 65, though targets are individualised.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman having sentinel node biopsy develops hypotension, rising airway pressure and a rash ten minutes after a blue dye injection. List the causes you would consider, describe how you would distinguish anaphylaxis from other causes, and outline immediate management if you suspect it.
markingGuide: Causes: drug effect, hypovolaemia, reduced venous return, anaphylaxis, obstructive and cardiac causes
Anaphylaxis clues: recent new drug, bronchospasm with rising airway pressure, flushing or rash, tachycardia, falling ETCO2
Call for help, stop trigger and volatile agent, 100% oxygen
Adrenaline early (IV titrated or IM per guidance) and rapid fluid
Serial mast cell tryptase and later allergy referral; check Resuscitation Council UK and Association of Anaesthetists guidance
questions.explanation: Considering mechanisms in a structured way prevents anchoring on a single cause. When anaphylaxis is suspected, adrenaline and trigger removal are time-critical.

questions.stem: Describe the minimum monitoring standards during general anaesthesia and in the recovery room, and explain why capnography is considered essential.
markingGuide: Trained anaesthetist present; same standard in recovery
Continuous pulse oximetry with audible tone, ECG, NIBP at least every 5 minutes
Capnography with airway device or general anaesthesia
Inspired oxygen, agent concentration, temperature and neuromuscular monitoring as appropriate
Capnography: confirms ventilation and tube position, detects disconnection, obstruction and circulatory events
Reference to Association of Anaesthetists standards; check current edition
questions.explanation: Monitoring standards are set to detect common critical events early. Capnography is the most reliable indicator of ventilation and airway position.
